title: Tech selloff deepens before the last big inflation report
dek: Nasdaq 100 futures are down more than 2% as Nvidia, Dell and other AI names extend Tuesday's losses and Asian chip stocks tumbled overnight. October PCE inflation and third-quarter GDP land at 8:30 a.m. ET, with a December Fed hike seen as nearly certain and reports of new US tariffs adding to the unease.
quick: S&P 500 futures are down roughly 1.4% to 1.7% and Nasdaq 100 futures about 2.3% to 2.6%, after Tuesday's 0.5% S&P drop and 1.5% Nasdaq slide.
Nvidia is down about 4.6% pre-market after falling about 6% Tuesday; Dell is down about 7% despite a blowout quarter and a $25 billion buyback.
Asian chip stocks sold off hard: SoftBank fell about 15%, Korea's Kospi about 6% and the Nikkei 2.8%.
Bloomberg and AP report the US is preparing new tariffs on China, the EU and 14 other economies; rates are not yet known.
October PCE inflation is expected at 3.8% a year (core 3.2%); futures price about a 96% to 97% chance of a Fed hike on December 9.
Markets are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early, at 1 p.m. ET, on Friday.

blocks.head: AI selling returns, led by Nvidia
blocks.what: Monday's relief rally on Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO lasted one day. On Tuesday the Nasdaq Composite fell 1.48% to 23,733.54 and the S&P 500 lost 0.50% to 7,201.09, while the Dow rose 0.85% to 50,018.70 as money moved into health care and consumer staples. Nvidia lost about 6% and is down another 4.6% or so pre-market. CNBC reported Huang told staff Nvidia does not need a succession plan, reviving concern about how much the company depends on him.
blocks.why: Nvidia is the largest weight in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, so its swings drive the indexes and chip suppliers worldwide.
blocks.watch: Huang faces a closed-door House hearing on December 1 and a public Senate hearing on December 3.

blocks.head: October PCE inflation and GDP at 8:30 a.m. ET
blocks.what: The Commerce Department releases October PCE prices, personal income and spending, plus the second estimate of third-quarter GDP, all moved up because of the holiday. Economists polled by Dow Jones expect headline PCE prices up 0.3% for the month and 3.8% from a year ago, up from 3.6%. Core PCE, which excludes food and energy, is expected up 0.3% for the month and 3.2% from a year earlier, versus 3.1%. GDP growth is forecast at a 3.5% annual rate.
blocks.why: This is the last major inflation report before the Fed's December 8-9 meeting. A hotter number would push Treasury yields and the dollar higher and could add pressure on richly valued tech stocks; a softer one could ease some of the hike talk for early next year.
blocks.watch: Also at 8:30: weekly jobless claims (forecast 201,000) and October durable goods orders (forecast up 0.7%).

blocks.head: Dell beats big, and the stock still falls
blocks.what: Dell reported third-quarter revenue of $54.9 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, and adjusted earnings of $9.45 a share versus about $6.59 expected, per its release and LSEG data. AI server orders were $60.2 billion and the AI backlog rose to $132.3 billion from $95 billion. It raised its full-year revenue forecast to about $202 billion and authorized $25 billion in buybacks. The stock, which fell about 11% in Tuesday's regular session, is down roughly 7% pre-market.
blocks.why: Selling on strong results signals investors are questioning how much AI demand is already in prices and how profitable AI servers are. That weighs on hardware, chip and data-center stocks.
blocks.watch: Workday, Autodesk and HP also beat forecasts but are lower or flat pre-market; see Stocks & Sectors.

blocks.head: New US tariffs reported to be coming
blocks.what: Bloomberg, AP and the WSJ report the administration is preparing higher tariffs on goods from China, the European Union and 14 other economies after a probe into subsidized and excess manufacturing capacity. The new duties would replace tariffs the Supreme Court struck down in February and would stack on the 10% to 12.5% tariffs announced earlier this year. Rates were not clear, Chinese goods are expected to face broader coverage, and an announcement could come as early as today, according to the reports.
blocks.why: Tariffs raise costs for importers and retailers and could feed into inflation just as the Fed is raising rates. Trade-exposed sectors, the euro and the yuan are most sensitive, and retaliation by the EU or China is a risk analysts cite.
blocks.watch: An official announcement and the rates chosen.

blocks.head: Anthropic slips below its IPO price
blocks.what: Anthropic shares fell 6.5% on Tuesday to $81.91, below their $83 IPO price less than a week after the November 19 debut, when the stock opened at $111.50, per Axios and CNBC.
blocks.why: The slide in the year's biggest IPO is being read as a gauge of investor appetite for AI.

blocks.head: Oil near three-month lows despite Gulf attacks
blocks.what: Brent fell about 1.7% to near $89.80 a barrel and WTI about 1.8% to near $80.60 in early European trade, per Anadolu. Iran says at least six tankers have been targeted in the Strait of Hormuz since Tuesday, and a Houthi attack on a Riyadh tower owned by Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund injured 11, per CNBC.
blocks.why: Lower oil helps the inflation outlook and transport stocks but weighs on energy shares. Markets are betting supply is ample even with Hormuz traffic reduced.

blocks.text: Asia

Asian tech stocks took the brunt of the renewed AI selling. Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 2.8% to about 57,012, giving back much of Tuesday's 4% jump, as SoftBank Group, a major OpenAI investor, plunged about 15%. In Seoul the Kospi fell about 6%, with Samsung Electronics down about 10% and SK Hynix about 11%, according to AP. Taiwan's Taiex dropped roughly 5% to 6%, with TSMC down sharply; reports differ on the exact close. Chinese markets were calmer: the Shanghai Composite slipped about 1%, and Hong Kong's Hang Seng ended roughly flat, with sources giving different final figures.
Europe

European stocks are holding up better. The Stoxx 600 is up about 0.3% to 0.5%, per Reuters. Carmakers are leading, with the autos index up nearly 4% after the EU capped hybrid vehicle imports starting December 1. Remy Cointreau jumped about 10% after setting long-term sales and profit targets. Chip stocks are the drag: ASML is down about 2%, ASM International about 2.7% and STMicroelectronics about 2.6%, and tech investor Prosus fell about 3.4% after a profit miss. The reported US tariff plans, which would hit the EU, are a cloud over exporters.
Currencies

The dollar is firmer before the PCE data, with the dollar index near 104, close to 19-month highs according to FXStreet. Hike bets and tariff news are supporting it. The euro is down about 0.2% near $1.094. The yen is little changed near 159 to 159.5 per dollar, just below the 160 level where traders watch for Japanese intervention. The pound is near $1.31 and the yuan near 6.67 per dollar, both little changed; the yuan is the currency most exposed if China-specific tariffs are confirmed.

US futures point to a sharply lower open, led by technology. As of the latest pre-market readings, S&P 500 futures were down about 1.4% to 1.7%, Nasdaq 100 futures about 2.3% to 2.6% and Dow futures about 0.8%, per CNBC and InvestingLive. The 8:30 a.m. data could shift them before the open. A drop of that size would put the S&P 500 near 7,080 to 7,100, still above last Friday's close of about 6,910 before Monday's 4.7% surge.

The pattern is the same as Tuesday but stronger: AI hardware and chip stocks are being sold, while defensive sectors held up. Tuesday's split was stark, with the Dow up 0.85% and the small-cap Russell 2000 up 0.57% even as the Nasdaq fell 1.5%.

Treasury yields are slightly lower this morning as stocks fall, per CNBC and Tradeweb data. The 2-year yield is near 4.63%, down about 4 basis points, and the 10-year near 4.85% to 4.87%, down 3 to 5 basis points. The 30-year closed Tuesday near 5.30%. The curve still slopes upward: the 10-year pays about 23 basis points more than the 2-year, and the 30-year about 45 basis points more than the 10-year.

Markets treat a December hike as close to certain. CME FedWatch data cited by several outlets show about a 96% to 97% chance of a quarter-point increase at the December 8-9 meeting, with about a 2% chance of a half point. Some reports also cite roughly a 60% chance of another hike in January. Officials have leaned that way: New York Fed President John Williams said Monday higher rates are likely needed over time, and Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said November 10 that inflation is broadening and more work is needed.
Fed events today

items: Michelle Bowman, Fed Vice Chair for Supervision: listed on economic calendars at 7:25 a.m. ET; topic not announced.
2 p.m. ET: The Fed's Beige Book, a survey of business conditions across the 12 Fed districts, the last one before the December meeting.

blocks.text: Sectors (Tuesday's session)

Technology was by far the weakest sector Tuesday, down about 3.3% as Nvidia, Micron and other chip stocks reversed part of Monday's rally. Industrials slipped about 0.5%. Every other sector rose, led by health care, up about 3%, helped by Insmed's 14% jump on Sanofi's $41 billion takeover and a broad move into defensive stocks. Consumer staples gained about 1.7% and real estate about 1.3%. Energy, financials and communication services each rose close to 1%.
Pre-market movers

items: Ambarella: down about 36% after a fourth-quarter sales forecast well below estimates.
Urban Outfitters: down about 14% to 15% after quarterly sales fell short of expectations.

Workday: down about 7% to 10%. Adjusted earnings of $2.82 a share and revenue of $2.71 billion beat forecasts and subscription revenue grew 12.8%, but CNBC tied the drop to disappointing free cash flow and a full-year sales outlook slightly below estimates.
Dell: down about 7% despite record results and higher guidance (see above).
Nvidia: down about 4.6%, extending Tuesday's roughly 6% loss.
Autodesk: down about 4%. It beat and raised its full-year outlook, but billings growth lagged revenue growth.

HP: little changed after volatile after-hours trading. It earned $0.83 a share on $16.0 billion revenue, above the $0.75 and $15.43 billion expected, and raised its dividend, but guided to lower free cash flow next year as memory chips rose to nearly 40% of its parts costs.
Deere: reported adjusted earnings of $3.89 a share, below the $4.03 expected, on revenue of $12.12 billion; it forecast fiscal 2027 net income of $4.5 billion to $5.25 billion.

blocks.text: Oil

Crude is lower, with Brent near $89.80 and WTI near $80.60, close to three-month lows and well below October's peak near $105. Supply is outweighing conflict risk. Gulf crude exports reached about 15 million barrels a day in October, around 82% of pre-war levels. Government inventory data is due at 10:30 a.m. ET, with analysts forecasting a build of about 2 million barrels.
Gold

Gold is near $3,530 to $3,560 an ounce, near its lowest level of the week after falling about 2% Tuesday, per FXStreet and Mining.com. Expectations of more Fed hikes and a firmer dollar make a metal that pays no interest less attractive. Gold is down more than a third from its January record above $5,500.
Crypto

Bitcoin is near $59,000, down about 2% over 24 hours, and Ether near $1,650, down about 2.5% to 3%, per Investing.com and crypto.news. Both are tracking tech stocks lower. Continued outflows from spot bitcoin ETFs and expected Fed hikes are the main drags cited. Traders are watching the year's low near $55,100, set last Saturday.
A packed morning because of the holiday. In order of likely market impact:

items: 8:30 a.m. ET, October PCE prices: core expected +0.3% for the month and 3.2% from a year ago; headline 3.8% a year. Personal income and spending are each forecast up 0.4%.
8:30 a.m. ET, third-quarter GDP, second estimate: forecast 3.5% annualized versus 3.4% first reported.
8:30 a.m. ET, weekly jobless claims: forecast 201,000 versus 203,000. Durable goods orders: forecast +0.7%.
10 a.m. ET, new home sales for October: forecast 650,000 at an annual rate, down from 676,000.
10:30 a.m. ET, government crude inventories; noon, natural gas storage.
Any time: a possible US tariff announcement on China, the EU and others.

blocks.text: A light day for new reports. Most of the action is reaction to Tuesday evening's tech results; no major S&P 500 companies are confirmed to report after today's close.

rows: Earnings missed while revenue beat. Watch management's comments on the farm downturn, tariffs and the fiscal 2027 profit outlook of $4.5 billion to $5.25 billion.
Whether the selloff deepens after a record quarter: investors are weighing AI server margins against a $132 billion AI backlog.
Free cash flow and the narrowed sales outlook; read-through for software spending and AI pressure on software firms.
Memory chip costs and PC demand into next year; lower free-cash-flow guidance.
Billings growth trailing revenue despite a raised outlook.
A roughly 36% drop on weak guidance; watch for spillover into smaller chip names.

blocks.text: Today carries most of the week's weight: the PCE, GDP, jobs and durable goods data at 8:30 a.m., the Beige Book at 2 p.m., and a possible tariff announcement. US stock and bond markets are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving. Friday is a shortened session, with stocks closing at 1 p.m. ET; the goods trade balance and wholesale inventories come out at 8:30 a.m., and early Black Friday sales reports will be watched for signs of how consumers are holding up after Tuesday's jump in Conference Board consumer confidence to 103.3. Looking past the week, Huang's congressional hearings on December 1 and 3 and the Fed decision on December 9 are the next big tests for markets.

bottom_line: The tone this morning is risk-off in tech, with AI-linked stocks under heavy selling from Tokyo to New York even after strong results from Dell, while bonds are steady and Europe is modestly higher. The 8:30 a.m. inflation data and any tariff news will set direction for a holiday-shortened week.
